title: From sentence vectors to attention
question: How did neural machine translation progress from fixed-length encoding through learned attention to the Transformer?

scope.summary: A six-paper reading map of architectural changes in neural machine translation, 2014–2017. It distinguishes phrase scoring, fixed-vector translation, recurrent attention, convolutional attention, and the Transformer.
scope.coverage: Six selected primary papers, seven recorded source versions, six results, and six proposed relationships. Full-text sections were checked on 2026-10-17; no scholarly reviewer has signed off.
scope.search_strategy: On 2026-10-17, used Neubig's tutorial (arXiv:1703.01619v1, sections 8.2–8.4) for orientation, then followed references in the six primary papers. Read pinned arXiv PDFs and checked their submission histories. Selected architectural changes relevant to the question; this is targeted reference tracing, not an exhaustive database search. ConvS2S v2 is pinned because Transformer v1 cites it explicitly.
exclusions: Earlier statistical MT and neural language models are background, not mapped comprehensively.
ByteNet, GNMT, Neural GPU, subword methods, and attention outside translation are omitted from this small map.
No post-2017 architectures, training reproduction, or cross-paper BLEU leaderboard.
gaps: Selection and relationship interpretation remain proposed and need a domain review.
Experimental data, tokenization, language pairs, model sizes, and decoding settings differ; numeric performance superiority is not inferred.
The teaching route places fixed-vector models together; it is not a priority claim. The timeline uses actual first-submission dates.

works.title: Learning Phrase Representations using RNN Encoder-Decoder for Statistical Machine Translation
Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate
Sequence to Sequence Learning with Neural Networks
Effective Approaches to Attention-based Neural Machine Translation

results.label: RNN phrase encoding
results.summary: A gated recurrent encoder compresses a phrase into a fixed-size vector. Its decoder scores target phrases as an additional feature for statistical translation.

settings.input: English–French phrase pairs and statistical machine translation.
settings.assumptions: Fixed-size phrase representation; gated recurrent encoder and decoder; phrase-based SMT integration.
settings.error: Translation evaluation is task-specific; no comparable numeric error or BLEU claim is extracted here.

results.label: Joint alignment
results.summary: A decoder learns a different weighted source context for each output step, reducing reliance on one fixed-length sentence representation.

settings.assumptions: Bidirectional recurrent encoding; learned soft alignment; autoregressive decoding.
settings.error: Translation evaluation is task-specific; no comparable numeric error or BLEU claim is extracted here.

results.label: LSTM sequence mapping
results.summary: A multilayer LSTM encodes a sentence into a vector for a second LSTM to decode. Reversing source token order is part of the reported setup.

settings.assumptions: Stacked LSTM encoder and decoder; fixed vector; reversed source order.
settings.error: Translation evaluation is task-specific; no comparable numeric error or BLEU claim is extracted here.

results.label: Global & local attention
results.summary: Studies global attention over all source positions and local attention over a selected window, with several alignment score functions.

settings.assumptions: Stacked recurrent encoder-decoder; global or local alignment; score-function choices.
settings.error: Translation evaluation is task-specific; no comparable numeric error or BLEU claim is extracted here.

results.label: Convolutional attention
results.summary: Convolutions replace recurrent state updates. Each decoder layer attends to source representations, allowing attention computation to be batched during training.

settings.input: WMT English–Romanian, English–German and English–French; summarization experiments excluded from this map.
settings.assumptions: Convolutional encoder-decoder; gated linear units; position embeddings; multi-step attention.
settings.error: Translation evaluation is task-specific; no comparable numeric error or BLEU claim is extracted here.

results.label: The Transformer
results.summary: Self-attention and feed-forward layers replace recurrence and convolution. Multi-head encoder-decoder attention retains access to source representations.

settings.assumptions: Multi-head attention; positional encodings; masked autoregressive decoder.
settings.cost: Table 1: self-attention layer O(n^2 d), O(1) sequential operations. This is a layer comparison, not total training or autoregressive decoding cost.
settings.error: Translation evaluation is task-specific; no comparable numeric error or BLEU claim is extracted here.

evidence.summary: Defines the conditional encoder-decoder model and its use in scoring phrase pairs. This version's author list has six names.
Identifies the fixed-vector bottleneck, describes the Cho-style model on which the architecture builds, and introduces learned alignment with a bidirectional encoder.
Describes sequence-to-sequence LSTMs and states that the model was developed in parallel with Cho et al.
Section 3.1 explicitly describes simplifying and generalizing Bahdanau-style attention; Section 3.2 introduces a local source window.

evidence.locator: Sections 2 and 3.3, PDF pages 2–4; Section 4.1, pages 4–5
evidence.summary: Contrasts its multiple attention hops with single-step recurrent attention, including Luong et al.; describes dot-product attention at each decoder layer.

evidence.locator: Sections 2, 3.2.3 and 4; PDF pages 2, 4–6; reference 9 on page 10
evidence.summary: Motivates shorter paths than convolutional models, cites ConvS2S v2, and explicitly connects encoder-decoder attention to Bahdanau-style models. Table 1 compares layer costs.

relations.summary: Bahdanau et al. address the fixed-vector bottleneck in the encoder-decoder formulation described in Section 2.1.
Sutskever et al. state that their model was developed in parallel with Cho et al.; this is not a claim of derivation.
Luong et al. explicitly describe a simpler attention path and additional alignment functions relative to Bahdanau et al.
Editorial interpretation: per-layer multi-hop attention extends the single-step pattern discussed alongside Luong et al. This is not a formal containment theorem.
Transformer Section 2 addresses distance-dependent convolutional paths using attention; the claim concerns architectural paths, not universal speed or accuracy.
Transformer Section 3.2.3 describes its encoder-decoder attention as following the source-attention pattern of earlier sequence models, explicitly including Bahdanau et al.

narrative.overview: Translation models first compressed a sentence into one representation. Attention let the decoder look back at its input. Later architectures changed how those representations were built, culminating in the Transformer.

turning_points.title: A sentence becomes a vector
turning_points.summary: Early encoder–decoder models learn fixed-length representations of phrases and sentences.

turning_points.title: The decoder learns where to look
turning_points.summary: Learned alignment replaces a single fixed context with access to source positions; global and local attention explore that choice.

turning_points.title: Rethink the sequence model
turning_points.summary: Convolution and then self-attention change the representation machinery. Their experimental settings still need to be compared carefully.
